title: Water Tank Size Calculator by Number of People + Table | Hacé Cuentas
h1: Water Tank Size Calculator: How Many Liters Do You Need?
description: Instantly find the right water tank capacity for your home. Enter the number of people and backup days — get liters needed and the closest commercial tank size.
answerSnippet: Water tank capacity formula: **Liters = people × 200 × reserve days**. A family of 4 with 1 backup day needs 800 L (buy a 1,000 L tank). With 2 backup days: 1,600 L (buy a 2,000 L tank). The 200 L/person/day standard is set by the WHO for full-plumbing urban households.
intro:
Choosing the wrong water tank size is one of the most common—and costly—mistakes in residential and commercial construction. Too small, and your household runs dry during municipal supply interruptions or peak demand periods. Too large, and you waste money on materials, installation, and the structural reinforcement needed to support excess weight. The consequences go beyond inconvenience: stagnant water in oversized tanks promotes bacterial growth, including *Legionella* and coliform bacteria, while undersized tanks leave families without water during emergencies, pressure drops, or scheduled maintenance cuts.

The industry standard for daily residential water consumption is **200 liters (53 US gallons) per person per day**, a figure endorsed by the World Health Organization (WHO) for basic sanitation adequacy and used as the baseline by plumbing codes across North America, Europe, and Latin America. However, real-world usage varies significantly: a household with low-flow fixtures, water-efficient appliances, and conscious conservation habits may use as little as 120–150 liters per person, while a home with a garden irrigation system, a pool top-up line, or multiple bathrooms in simultaneous use can exceed 300 liters per person daily.

Backup reserve days are equally critical. Urban properties connected to a reliable municipal network typically size for **1 day of autonomy**—enough to bridge a standard overnight or weekend maintenance window. Suburban and peri-urban homes, where supply interruptions can last 24–48 hours without warning, should plan for **2–3 days**. Rural properties on well systems or areas prone to infrastructure failures may need **4–7 days** of stored capacity, especially if the household includes vulnerable members who depend on uninterrupted water access for medical reasons.

This calculator applies the universally accepted formula—**Capacity (L) = People × Daily consumption (L) × Reserve days**—to give you an immediate, actionable tank size. It's designed for homeowners planning a new build or renovation, plumbing contractors verifying system specs, civil engineering students working through hydraulic design problems, and anyone who needs a fast sanity check before ordering equipment.
keyTakeaway: Formula: **L = people × 200 × reserve days**. A family of 4 with 2 backup days needs 1,600 L — buy a standard 2,000 L tank.

explanation:
## How Water Tank Capacity Is Calculated

The standard formula accepted by WHO, ICC, and most national plumbing codes is:

**Liters needed = number of people × 200 L/day × backup days**

The 200 L/person/day figure covers all typical household uses: drinking (2–3 L), cooking (5–10 L), toilet flushing (30–50 L), showering (60–80 L), laundry (30–50 L), and dishwashing/cleaning (~15–25 L).

## Quick Reference Table: Liters by Household Size

| People | 1 backup day | 2 backup days | 3 backup days |
|--------|-------------|---------------|---------------|
| 1 | 200 L | 400 L | 600 L |
| 2 | 400 L | 800 L | 1,200 L |
| 3 | 600 L | 1,200 L | 1,800 L |
| 4 | 800 L | 1,600 L | 2,400 L |
| 5 | 1,000 L | 2,000 L | 3,000 L |
| 6 | 1,200 L | 2,400 L | 3,600 L |
| 8 | 1,600 L | 3,200 L | 4,800 L |
| 10 | 2,000 L | 4,000 L | 6,000 L |

*Always buy the next commercially available size up (500 / 750 / 1,000 / 1,100 / 1,500 / 2,000 / 2,500 / 3,000 / 5,000 L).*

## Reserve Days: Which Is Right for You?

- **1 day** — Urban home with reliable municipal supply
- **2–3 days** — Suburban area with occasional interruptions
- **4–7 days** — Rural property, well system, or frequent outages

## Key Factors for Installation

- **Tank material**: High-density polyethylene (triple-wall) is most common and durable
- **Placement**: Always on a solid, level reinforced base — water weighs 1 kg/L
- **Elevation for gravity pressure**: 10 m of head ≈ 1 bar; most homes need a booster pump
- **Safety margin**: Add 10–20% — buy the next commercial size up from your calculated minimum

## Important Disclaimer

This calculator is a planning reference. For building permits, code compliance, or critical systems, consult a licensed plumber or structural engineer.

faq.q: How much water does one person use per day, and where does the 200-liter figure come from?
faq.a: The 200-liter (53 US gallon) per-person-per-day figure is the internationally recognized standard for residential water consumption in urban settings with full plumbing infrastructure. It accounts for drinking (2–3 L), cooking (5–10 L), toilet flushing (30–50 L), showering (60–80 L), laundry (30–50 L), dishwashing (15–25 L), and general cleaning. The World Health Organization (WHO) uses this benchmark in its sanitation planning guidelines. In practice, water-efficient households may use 120–150 L per person per day, while homes with gardens or pools may reach 250–350 L.

faq.q: How many backup days should I plan for?
faq.a: Urban properties with reliable municipal supply: 1 day. Suburban areas with periodic interruptions: 2–3 days. Rural properties on well systems, especially prone to power outages: 3–7 days. If anyone in the household has medical needs requiring uninterrupted water (dialysis, wound care), always size for at least 3 days regardless of location.

faq.q: What commercial tank sizes are available, and which should I buy?
faq.a: Standard commercial polyethylene tanks are available in these sizes: 500 L, 750 L, 1,000 L, 1,100 L, 1,500 L, 2,000 L, 2,500 L, 3,000 L, and 5,000 L. Always buy the first size equal to or above your calculated minimum — never size down to save money. The extra margin also acts as a buffer for peak-demand days and guests.

faq.q: Should I add a safety margin on top of the calculated capacity?
faq.a: Yes, most plumbing engineers recommend adding a 10–20% safety margin above the calculated minimum. This buffer accounts for peak-demand days (weekends, holidays, houseguests), seasonal increases in hot months, and the fact that tanks are never fully drained in practice. Since commercial tanks are sold in fixed increments, you're already rounding up — but if you're between sizes, always go to the next one.

faq.q: What are the most common tank materials, and which should I choose?
faq.a: **HDPE (high-density polyethylene / triple-wall)** — most popular worldwide: lightweight, UV-resistant, corrosion-proof, easy to install, wide size range. **Fiberglass (GRP)** — stronger, better for underground installations, costs more, needs professional handling. **Stainless steel** — ideal for food service or medical facilities, expensive. **Reinforced concrete cisterns** — permanent, cost-effective at 10,000 L+, requires professional construction. For standard residential use, UV-stabilized polyethylene is the best balance of cost, durability, and ease of maintenance.

faq.q: How high does my tank need to be to achieve good water pressure?
faq.a: Water pressure from a gravity-fed tank: **1 meter of head ≈ 0.098 bar (1.42 psi)**. For acceptable pressure of 1–2 bar (15–30 psi), your tank water surface needs to be 10–20 meters above your fixtures — rarely achievable with a standard rooftop tank. Most single-family homes achieve only 3–6 m of head (0.3–0.6 bar), which is adequate for gravity-fed showers but insufficient for instant water heaters or washing machines requiring 1.5–2 bar minimum. A pressure booster pump on the outlet line is standard in most modern systems.

faq.q: How often should I clean my water tank, and what's the correct procedure?
faq.a: Health authorities recommend cleaning and disinfecting residential tanks every 6–12 months, or immediately after any contamination event. Procedure: (1) Shut inlet valve and drain completely. (2) Scrub interior with a stiff brush and a 1:100 bleach-to-water solution. (3) Rinse thoroughly twice. (4) Refill and add final disinfection: ~1 mL household bleach per 100 L of tank capacity. (5) Stand 30 minutes, then flush distribution lines until chlorine smell dissipates. Keep a cleaning log.

faq.q: What structural considerations apply for large tanks?
faq.a: Water weighs 1 kg/L (1 metric ton per 1,000 L). A full 3,000 L tank weighs approximately 3,050 kg. Rooftop installations require a structural engineering assessment — most residential slabs are rated 150–300 kg/m², easily exceeded by a large tank on a small footprint. Ground-level tanks need a reinforced concrete pad (15–20 cm thick with rebar). For tanks larger than 2,000 L, always consult a structural engineer before installation.

faq.q: Can I connect two tanks together to reach the capacity I need?
faq.a: Yes, parallel tank connections are standard when your required capacity exceeds what a single tank provides. Use equal-diameter pipes and balanced valve arrangements so all tanks fill and drain at the same rate. Install individual shutoff valves on each tank so you can isolate one for cleaning while the others remain in service. Tanks must be installed at exactly the same elevation — even a 2–3 cm height difference causes flow imbalance in a passive gravity system.

faq.q: Does stored water lose quality over time, and how do I prevent it?
faq.a: Yes. Residual chlorine dissipates within 24–72 hours, after which bacterial inhibition stops. UV light through translucent tanks promotes algae growth. To maintain water quality: (1) Use opaque, UV-stabilized tanks. (2) Position the inlet at the bottom or side for full circulation. (3) Install a screen on the inlet. (4) Maintain 0.2–0.5 mg/L residual chlorine if water is stored longer than 24 hours (test with a pool kit). (5) Right-size your tank — oversized tanks with low daily turnover are a greater contamination risk.

faq.q: Are there building codes or permits required for water tank installation?
faq.a: Yes. In the US, the International Plumbing Code (IPC) and International Residential Code (IRC) set baseline standards with state/municipal variations. In Canada, the National Plumbing Code (NPC) applies. In the UK, the Water Supply (Water Fittings) Regulations 1999 govern tank installation. In Australia, the Plumbing Code of Australia (PCA) sets minimum standards. In most jurisdictions, a permit is required for new tank installations, and work must be performed or inspected by a licensed plumber. Always check with your local building department.

faq.q: How do I size a tank if I also have a garden, pool, or livestock?
faq.a: The standard formula covers only household use. Add each additional demand separately: garden drip irrigation ≈ 1–4 L/hour per emitter; standard garden hose at full flow ≈ 15–20 L/minute; dairy cow ≈ 80–150 L/day; horse ≈ 25–50 L/day; sheep/goat ≈ 5–15 L/day; pool top-up ≈ 1–3% of pool volume per week in warm climates. Add these to your household base, multiply by reserve days, and apply a 15% safety margin.
